title: How Hip-hop Works
summary: Selects edition of Stuff You Should Know, with Josh picking the July 2013 episode "How Hip-hop Works." The hosts explain that hip hop is a broader culture (graffiti, MCing/rapping, DJing, breakdancing and other dance, and style/fashion) of which rap music is one part. They trace roots from West African griot traditions and the slave ships, through church, jazz, blues and calypso, to Jamaican sound systems, toasting, and dub, then to Clive Campbell (DJ Cool Herc) in the Bronx, the break beat, early MCs like Coke La Rock, and the Zulu Nation. They cover the early 1980s rise of rap records (Sugarhill Gang's "Rapper's Delight"), MTV, gangster rap (N.W.A), regional scenes (Dirty South, Wu-Tang), graffiti origins with Taki 183 and Hayes, breakdancing history including the moonwalk and the Harlem Shake, and hip hop fashion and commercialization. The episode closes with listener mail from France and Israel.

segments.title: Selects intro and hosts' banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this Selects pick, How Hip Hop Works from July 2013, and the hosts joke about DJs and whether they have business talking about hip hop.

segments.title: Hip hop vs. rap and who coined the term
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish hip hop as a broader cultural movement from rap, which is one music form within it. They note several people credited with coining the term 'hip hop', with its first print use in the Village Voice.
topics: origin of the term hip hop

segments.title: The four elements of hip hop
segments.summary: A cultural historian's four pillars are named: DJing, MCing/rapping, breakdancing and other movement, graffiti and visual art, and style and fashion. Crumping is mentioned as a dance style.

segments.title: African and West Indian roots
segments.summary: The hosts trace hip hop's roots to West Africa, including griot storytelling set to drums and dance, carried on slave ships to the West Indies. Church, gospel, calypso, salsa, jazz and blues influenced it, and the music reached Jamaica through American soldiers in World War Two.

segments.title: Jamaican sound systems, toasting, and dub
segments.summary: Jamaican DJs with portable sound systems played street and block parties and started toasting, a talk-over style that evolved into early rap. Dub, a remix-style reggae form with echo and bass, is also described.

segments.title: Clive Campbell becomes DJ Cool Herc in the Bronx
segments.summary: Clive Campbell moved to the Bronx in 1967 and became DJ Cool Herc, widely called the originator of hip hop. He drew crowds to parties as a known graffiti tagger, and he developed the break beat by looping two copies of the same record. Cool Herc also began toasting, and with Coke La Rock he launched rapping.

segments.title: Early DJs, b-boys, and the Zulu Nation
segments.summary: Afrika Bambaataa, born Kevin Donovan, formed the Zulu Nation as a positive alternative to gangs. Grandmaster Flash, born Joseph Sadler, was an innovator who built an early crossfader and developed punch phrasing. Grand Wizard Theodore is credited with scratching, and beatboxing is described.

segments.title: Early recordings, radio, MCs and crossover to the 1980s
segments.summary: Hip hop moved from parties to recordings and radio, with Mr. Magic's Rap Attack in New York as an early show. MCs rose to the front, and DJ Jazzy Jeff and the Fresh Prince addressed the confusion over roles. Sugar Hill Gang's 'Rapper's Delight' became the first hit rap record. Blondie's 'Rapture', Run-DMC, LL Cool J, Beastie Boys and others crossed over, and MTV Raps was launched.
topics: DJ Jazzy Jeff and the Fresh Prince

segments.title: Gangster rap, regional scenes and later artists
segments.summary: Gangster rap, led by N.W.A, changed the focus of the genre from the original positive, playful themes. The hosts discuss Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg, Ice Cube, and groups including A Tribe Called Quest, De La Soul, Wu-Tang Clan, Gang Starr, and Public Enemy. Southern scenes including 2 Live Crew, Outkast, and Goodie Mob and the Dirty South are noted, along with rap-rock crossovers.

segments.title: Graffiti origins: Taki 183 and Hayes
segments.summary: Graffiti tagging is described as a part of hip hop that came first. Taki 183, a Greek-American messenger in the 1960s, is credited with early tagging, and the 1971 New York Times article on him is mentioned. Cool Herc was also a tagger, and the artist Hayes is noted for album covers and graffiti. Graffiti became gallery art in the 1970s.

segments.title: Breakdancing, moonwalk, and the Harlem Shake
segments.summary: Breakdancing is traced to West African movement, the cakewalk, Lindy Hop, Charleston, and martial arts influences. Old footage suggests breakdancing and the moonwalk existed before the 1980s, with James Brown's moves cited as an influence. The hosts also discuss the 1980s breakdancing boom and the Harlem Shake online craze.

segments.title: Hip hop fashion and commercialization
segments.summary: Hip hop fashion is described, from comfortable loose clothing and Adidas with Run-DMC to gold chains, grills, and baggy clothes linked to prison wear. Russell Simmons' Phat Farm and rap moguls as brands are mentioned, and the hosts say hip hop is now a global product.

segments.title: Mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Listener mail from Julie in France and Daniel in Israel, who says his boss listens to the show, followed by the standard sign-off.
